name: Brachial artery
func: The main artery of the upper arm. It carries blood from the armpit down to the elbow, where it splits to supply the forearm and hand. It's the artery used when blood pressure is measured with a cuff.

levels.kid:
When a nurse puts a squeezy cuff around your upper arm to check your blood pressure, they're listening to your **brachial artery**!

It's the big blood tube running down the inside of your upper arm, from your armpit to your elbow. "Brachial" just means "arm."

At the bend of your elbow, it splits into two smaller tubes that carry blood all the way to your fingers.

If you press gently on the inside of your elbow, just to the pinky side of the strong cord in the middle (that's a tendon), you might feel it thumping.
levels.hs:
The **brachial artery** is the continuation of the **axillary artery**. It gets its new name at the lower border of the **teres major** muscle, at the bottom of the armpit, and runs down the **inner (medial) side of the upper arm** in a groove between the **biceps** in front and the **triceps** behind.

It travels with the **median nerve**, which starts on its outer side, crosses in front of it around the middle of the arm, and ends up on its inner side at the elbow. Paired veins (venae comitantes) wrap around it.

In the upper arm it gives off the **profunda brachii (deep brachial) artery**, which spirals around the back of the humerus with the **radial nerve** to supply the triceps.

At the elbow it lies in a triangular hollow called the **cubital fossa**, medial to the **biceps tendon** and protected by a fibrous sheet (the **bicipital aponeurosis**). Just below the elbow, at the level of the neck of the radius, it divides into the **radial artery** (thumb side) and the **ulnar artery** (little-finger side).

This is where a **stethoscope** is placed to hear blood pressure sounds when a cuff is deflated.
levels.college:
Branches: the **profunda brachii** (with the radial nerve in the radial groove), the **nutrient artery of the humerus**, muscular branches, and the **superior and inferior ulnar collateral arteries**. These collaterals form a rich **anastomosis around the elbow** with recurrent branches of the radial and ulnar arteries, so the brachial artery can be tied off below the profunda origin without the forearm dying, though suddenly blocking it is still dangerous.

Relations at the cubital fossa (lateral to medial): **radial nerve** (under the brachioradialis edge), **biceps tendon**, **brachial artery**, **median nerve**. The **median cubital vein**, the most common site for drawing blood, lies superficial to the bicipital aponeurosis, which separates it from the artery and nerve.

The brachial artery can be **compressed against the humerus** in the middle of the arm to control bleeding further down.

**Blood pressure** measurement: inflating the cuff above systolic pressure stops flow; as it deflates, turbulent flow produces **Korotkoff sounds**. The pressure when sounds first appear (phase I) is **systolic**; when they disappear (phase V) is **diastolic**. A cuff that's too small overestimates pressure.

Variations are common: in about 10–20% of arms there's a **high division**, with the radial or ulnar artery arising in the upper arm. A **superficial brachial artery** can be mistaken for a vein during injections.
levels.phd:
The brachial artery is a key research window into **endothelial function**. In **flow-mediated dilation (FMD)**, a forearm cuff is inflated for about 5 minutes and released; the resulting surge of blood (reactive hyperemia) increases **shear stress** on the brachial endothelium, triggering **nitric oxide** release via shear-activated **endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS)** (phosphorylated through the PI3K/Akt pathway and calcium signaling). Ultrasound measures how much the artery widens, typically 5–10% in healthy young adults.

Reduced FMD is an early marker of **endothelial dysfunction**: it appears in smokers, people with high cholesterol, diabetes or hypertension, and even in healthy-looking adolescents with risk factors, before any plaque forms. It's linked to reduced NO bioavailability from **eNOS uncoupling** (when its cofactor tetrahydrobiopterin is oxidized, eNOS makes superoxide instead of NO) and from NO being destroyed by reactive oxygen species. Exercise training improves FMD, a direct demonstration of how activity protects arteries.

The brachial artery is a **muscular (distributing) artery**: a thick smooth-muscle media between the internal and external elastic laminae, more able to change diameter than the elastic aorta.

Central (aortic) systolic pressure is usually lower than brachial systolic pressure because of **pulse pressure amplification**: reflected waves and stiffer, narrower arteries make the pulse peak taller as it travels outward. Devices estimate central pressure from the brachial waveform using transfer functions, since central pressure may better predict organ damage.
levels.expert:
**Supracondylar fractures of the humerus**, common in children after falling on an outstretched hand, can kink, compress or tear the brachial artery. Look for a **pale, pulseless hand**, delayed capillary refill and worsening pain. Untreated ischemia leads to **compartment syndrome** of the forearm and **Volkmann's ischemic contracture** (a clawed, stiff hand from muscle death). Pain on passive finger extension is an early warning sign of compartment syndrome. The **median nerve** and its **anterior interosseous branch** (weak "OK sign") are often injured too.

The brachial pulse is used in **infants** to check circulation during resuscitation.

The artery is an access route for cardiac catheterization and endovascular procedures, including some **neurointerventional** cases when femoral access is impossible, though the radial artery has largely replaced it because complications are fewer. Brachial puncture risks hematoma compressing the median nerve.

**Arteriovenous fistulas** for dialysis are often created by joining the brachial artery to the cephalic vein at the elbow.

Blood pressure pearls: always check both arms (a difference above about 15 mmHg suggests subclavian or aortic disease); use the right cuff size; measure seated with the arm supported at heart level.

Imaging: duplex ultrasound, CT angiography or catheter angiography in trauma. Treatment in general terms: urgent fracture reduction, which often restores the pulse; surgical exploration and repair (sometimes with a vein graft) if the hand stays poorly perfused; and fasciotomy for compartment syndrome.

keyPoints: Continuation of the axillary artery from the lower border of teres major
Runs on the medial arm with the median nerve
Profunda brachii travels with the radial nerve
Divides into radial and ulnar arteries in the cubital fossa
Used for blood pressure measurement (Korotkoff sounds)
Supracondylar fracture risks brachial injury and Volkmann's contracture

test.q: The brachial artery divides into which two arteries?
test.explain: It splits in the cubital fossa, usually at the level of the radial neck.

test.q: The brachial artery begins at the lower border of which muscle?
test.explain: At teres major's lower border, the axillary artery becomes the brachial artery.

test.q: Which nerve travels alongside the brachial artery down the arm?
test.explain: The median nerve crosses the artery from lateral to medial during its descent.

test.q: A child with a supracondylar fracture has a cold, pale hand. The vessel at most risk is the:
test.explain: The brachial artery lies right in front of the distal humerus and can be kinked or torn.

test.q: The sounds heard over the brachial artery when measuring blood pressure are ______ sounds.
test.explain: Phase I marks systolic pressure; phase V (disappearance) marks diastolic.
